title: Labels and the table
subtitle: Reading Burgundy and eating with it

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: A Burgundy label shows the appellation, from Bourgogne to Grand Cru, the producer, the vintage, and whether it's a domaine or négociant. Mis en bouteille au domaine means estate-bottled. Monopole means a single owner holds the whole vineyard, like La Romanée-Conti. Vieilles vignes means old vines, but it isn't legally defined.

steps.title: Vintage
steps.body: Because Burgundy is continental and risky, vintage matters a lot. Frost, hail and rain can halve a crop or dilute it. Warm vintages give riper, rounder wines; cool ones leaner, fresher wines. Good producers make good wine even in difficult years.

steps.prompt: What does monopole mean on a Burgundy label?
options: A single owner holds the whole vineyard
steps.explanation: A monopole belongs to one owner.

steps.title: At the table
steps.body: Red Burgundy suits roast chicken, duck, game birds, boeuf bourguignon and coq au vin, two dishes cooked with the region's wine. Époisses cheese suits both reds and whites. Chablis suits oysters and snails, escargots de Bourgogne; Meursault suits lobster and creamy chicken. Serve reds at 14 to 16 degrees.

steps.prompt: Vieilles vignes is a legally defined term in Burgundy.
steps.explanation: Not true. It means old vines, but there's no legal definition.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Labels show appellation, producer and vintage
Vintage matters greatly in continental Burgundy
Red Burgundy suits coq au vin; Chablis suits oysters
